messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi Patel, a 42-year-old tax inspector, came to treatment nearly a year after a car accident in which he had seriously injured another driver. He had been driving home after a long day, distracted for a moment at an intersection, when his car struck the side of a smaller vehicle. What remained with him most sharply was not a complete sequence but fragments: the metallic impact, the sudden blare of a horn, and, above all, the sound that followed from the other car—shouting and crying that he still heard in his head at unexpected moments. Some parts of the scene were unnaturally vivid, like the crushed driver’s door and the other man’s face as people gathered; other stretches were simply absent. Ravi could recount a few seconds with painful clarity and then hit a blank space that left him feeling as if the worst part might be missing.

In the months afterward, he became preoccupied with what the accident meant about him. He had come to believe that he had failed in a basic duty to protect other people, and this belief carried a deep sense of humiliation. He was certain he had exposed something unforgivable in himself. Just as disturbing was the feeling that the world no longer followed the ordinary rules he had trusted—that a routine drive home, a mundane evening, could turn in an instant into irreversible harm. Those conclusions seemed to shape the way he remembered the crash. He returned again and again to the most condemning fragments, while the gaps in memory grew more menacing to him; the missing parts felt less like ordinary incomplete recall and more like proof that something even worse had happened, something that would confirm how badly he had failed.

That broken quality of memory, in turn, strengthened the way he judged himself. Because he could hear the cries and the horn as if they were happening again, while whole sections stayed blank, Ravi experienced the accident as unfinished in his mind. He would think, if he could not even hold the event together properly, then he did not deserve to move past it. The sharply preserved moments seemed to him like evidence for the prosecution; the missing moments left room for his imagination to fill in further blame. He did not describe confusion so much as moral certainty: whatever he could not remember, he assumed it reflected his failure.

His daily life as a tax inspector gave him little room to escape reminders. Driving to field visits, he found himself slowing abruptly whenever he saw a car with side-panel damage or fresh dents, and the sight could pull up the same split-second image of impact along with the remembered sounds. If colleagues casually asked about the accident or if conversation touched on traffic injuries, he would feel his body tense before he said very little. Funerals became especially difficult. When an older relative died, Ravi stood at the cemetery hearing prayers while his attention fixed on the nearness of graves and grieving families; the atmosphere fused instantly with his sense that someone else had nearly died because of him. These reminders set off a familiar effort to clamp down on his mind. He tried hard not to think about the crash at all, and when the images broke through he told himself he deserved the distress. At other moments he would mutter that it could have been worse, that at least the man had survived, but the comparison brought only brief relief and never settled anything.

Over time those habits tightened around him. The more he pushed the memories away, the more jaggedly they seemed to return, attached to damaged cars, grief rituals, or any direct mention of the event. He began taking longer routes to avoid the intersection where the collision had happened and dreading workdays that required driving across town. At home, his wife noticed that he went silent whenever family members discussed illness, funerals, or accidents. Yet his private way of handling it—insisting he should suffer, trying to shut the memories down, reminding himself others had it worse—left him feeling even more disgraced. If he still needed to punish himself, he reasoned, that only proved the depth of his failure. And each new surge of shame made the memory fragments feel harsher and more accusatory the next time they came.

By the time Ravi sought help, he was exhausted by how little space remained in his life. A recent cemetery service for a family friend had left him hearing the crash sounds for the rest of the day, and the following week he had to pull his car over on the way to an inspection after seeing a vehicle that had been hit at the side. What frightened him most was the thought that this was now permanent—that he was the kind of man who had failed to protect another person and should not be allowed peace. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to find some way to remember what happened without feeling condemned by it every time.
